script: Today, let's talk about honeybees and how they share information. When a bee finds a good group of flowers, it flies back to the hive. But how does it tell the other bees where the flowers are? Bees can't talk, of course. Instead, they dance. Scientists call this the waggle dance. The bee walks in a straight line and shakes its body from side to side. Then it turns around and does it again, many times. The direction of the straight line tells the other bees which way to fly. The length of the waggle tells them how far away the flowers are. A longer waggle means the flowers are farther away. Now, if the flowers are very close to the hive, the bee does a different dance. It just moves around in a small circle. This is called the round dance. It simply means, the food is near, so go out and look around. I think this is amazing. Such a small animal can share clear information with the other bees in its hive. Next time, we'll look at how bees make honey from the nectar they collect.

translation: 오늘은 꿀벌과 꿀벌이 정보를 나누는 방법에 대해 이야기해 봅시다. 벌이 괜찮은 꽃 무리를 찾으면 벌집으로 날아 돌아옵니다. 그런데 다른 벌들에게 꽃이 어디 있는지 어떻게 알려 줄까요? 물론 벌은 말을 할 수 없습니다. 대신 춤을 춥니다. 과학자들은 이것을 '8자 춤(waggle dance)'이라고 부릅니다. 벌은 직선으로 걸으면서 몸을 좌우로 흔듭니다. 그런 다음 돌아서 다시 이것을 여러 번 반복합니다. 직선의 방향은 다른 벌들에게 어느 쪽으로 날아가야 하는지 알려 줍니다. 몸을 흔드는 길이는 꽃이 얼마나 멀리 있는지 알려 줍니다. 더 길게 흔들수록 꽃이 더 멀리 있다는 뜻입니다. 그런데 꽃이 벌집에 아주 가까우면 벌은 다른 춤을 춥니다. 그냥 작은 원을 그리며 돕니다. 이것을 '원형 춤'이라고 합니다. 이 춤은 단순히 '먹이가 가까이 있으니 나가서 둘러봐'라는 뜻입니다. 저는 이게 정말 놀랍다고 생각합니다. 이렇게 작은 동물이 벌집의 다른 벌들과 분명한 정보를 나눌 수 있으니까요. 다음 시간에는 벌이 모아 온 꽃꿀로 꿀을 만드는 방법을 살펴보겠습니다.

script: Good morning. Today's topic is the Moon. Have you ever noticed that the Moon seems to change shape during the month? Sometimes it's a full circle, and sometimes it's just a thin line. But the Moon itself doesn't really change. It is always a round ball. So why does it look different? The answer is sunlight. The Moon doesn't make its own light. It reflects light from the Sun. Half of the Moon is always lit by the Sun, but we can't always see that half from Earth. As the Moon travels around Earth, we see different amounts of the bright side. When the Moon is between Earth and the Sun, the bright side faces away from us, so we see almost nothing. This is called a new moon. When Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, we can see the whole bright side. That's a full moon. The trip around Earth takes about twenty-nine and a half days. That's why the full moon comes back about once a month. For homework, please look at the Moon every night this week and draw its shape in your notebook.

script: Today, we're going to talk about volcanoes. A volcano is an opening in the Earth's surface. Deep under the ground, it's very, very hot. It's so hot that rock melts. This melted rock is called magma. Magma is lighter than the solid rock around it, so it slowly moves up. When magma comes out of a volcano, we call it lava. So magma and lava are the same material. The name just changes when it reaches the surface. Now, not all volcanoes are the same. Some volcanoes explode with great force. They throw ash and rocks high into the sky. Other volcanoes are much quieter. Their lava flows out slowly, like thick soup. The volcanoes in Hawaii are good examples of this quiet type. People can sometimes walk near the lava and take pictures, with a guide, of course. So why are some volcanoes quiet and others violent? One big reason is gas. When magma has a lot of gas trapped inside it, the pressure builds up, and then the volcano explodes. It's a bit like shaking a bottle of soda and then opening it quickly.

translation: 오늘은 화산에 대해 이야기하겠습니다. 화산은 지구 표면에 난 구멍입니다. 땅속 깊은 곳은 아주, 아주 뜨겁습니다. 너무 뜨거워서 바위가 녹을 정도예요. 이렇게 녹은 바위를 마그마라고 합니다. 마그마는 주변의 단단한 바위보다 가벼워서 천천히 위로 올라옵니다. 마그마가 화산 밖으로 나오면 용암이라고 부릅니다. 그러니까 마그마와 용암은 같은 물질입니다. 지표면에 도달하면 이름만 바뀌는 거예요. 그런데 모든 화산이 같지는 않습니다. 어떤 화산은 엄청난 힘으로 폭발합니다. 화산재와 돌을 하늘 높이 던져 올리죠. 다른 화산들은 훨씬 조용합니다. 용암이 걸쭉한 수프처럼 천천히 흘러나옵니다. 하와이의 화산들이 이런 조용한 유형의 좋은 예입니다. 사람들이 때로는 용암 가까이 걸어가서 사진을 찍기도 합니다. 물론 가이드와 함께요. 그럼 왜 어떤 화산은 조용하고 어떤 화산은 격렬할까요? 한 가지 큰 이유는 가스입니다. 마그마 안에 가스가 많이 갇혀 있으면 압력이 쌓이고, 결국 화산이 폭발합니다. 탄산음료 병을 흔든 다음 빨리 여는 것과 조금 비슷하죠.

script: Let's talk about the piano today. Most of you know this instrument, but do you know where its name comes from? About three hundred years ago, an Italian man named Bartolomeo Cristofori built a new keyboard instrument. Before that, a popular keyboard instrument was the harpsichord. The harpsichord had one problem. When you pressed a key, a small piece inside plucked the string. It made a nice sound, but the sound was always about the same volume. You couldn't play softly or loudly. Cristofori's instrument was different. Inside, small hammers hit the strings. If you pressed a key gently, the sound was soft. If you pressed it hard, the sound was loud. So he gave it a name that means soft and loud. In Italian, that's pianoforte. Over time, people made the name shorter, and now we just say piano. This change was very important for music. Composers could now write music with strong feelings, going from quiet to loud in one piece. In our next class, I'll play a harpsichord recording and a piano recording, so you can hear the difference yourselves.

script: Today, I want to talk about something we all do every day: throwing away food. In many countries, about one third of all food is wasted. When food waste goes to a landfill, it is buried under lots of other trash. There isn't much air down there. Without air, the food breaks down slowly and makes a gas called methane. Methane is a greenhouse gas. It traps heat in the air and makes the planet warmer. So, what can we do? One easy answer is composting. Composting means putting food scraps, like fruit peels and old vegetables, in a special bin with dry leaves and air. Tiny living things, like bacteria and worms, eat the food. After a few months, the food turns into dark, rich soil. Farmers and gardeners love this soil because it helps plants grow. Our university started a composting program last year. There are green bins in every dining hall. In the first year, we composted about forty tons of food. That's a lot of waste that didn't go to a landfill. So please, the next time you finish your lunch, look for the green bin.

script: OK, let's get started. Last week we discussed how memories are formed. Today I want to look at one thing that affects memory more than most students realize: sleep. Many of you probably stay up late before an exam, trying to study as much as possible. It seems logical, right? More study time should mean better results. But research suggests the opposite. In one common type of experiment, researchers teach two groups of people a list of new words. One group then gets a full night of sleep. The other group stays awake. The next day, both groups take a test. Again and again, the group that slept remembers more words. Why? During sleep, especially deep sleep, the brain seems to replay what we learned during the day. It moves information from short-term storage into long-term memory. You can think of it like saving a document on your computer. If you don't save it, your work may disappear. So, what does this mean for you? Well, studying is important, of course, but cutting your sleep to study may actually hurt your performance. A better plan is to study over several days and then get a good night's rest before the test.

script: Today we're starting our unit on prehistoric art, and I want to begin with one of the most famous discoveries in art history. In 1940, four teenagers in southwestern France were exploring the countryside when they found a narrow hole in the ground. They climbed inside and discovered a cave covered with hundreds of paintings. This is the Lascaux cave. The paintings are around seventeen thousand years old. Most of them show animals, such as horses, deer, and wild cattle. Interestingly, there are very few pictures of people. So how did artists paint in a dark cave so long ago? They made colors from natural materials. Red and yellow came from minerals in the ground, and black came from charcoal. They mixed these powders with water or animal fat. Some paint was put on with brushes made of animal hair, and some was blown through hollow bones, a bit like a spray. For light, they burned animal fat in small stone lamps. Sadly, after the cave was opened to the public, the breath of thousands of visitors changed the air inside, and the paintings began to get damaged. So the cave was closed in 1963. Today, visitors can see a very accurate copy built nearby.

translation: 오늘은 선사 시대 미술 단원을 시작하는데, 미술사에서 가장 유명한 발견 중 하나로 시작하고 싶습니다. 1940년, 프랑스 남서부에서 네 명의 10대가 시골을 탐험하다가 땅에 난 좁은 구멍을 발견했습니다. 그들이 안으로 기어 들어가 보니 수백 점의 그림으로 덮인 동굴이 있었습니다. 이것이 라스코 동굴입니다. 그림들은 약 1만 7천 년 전의 것입니다. 대부분은 말, 사슴, 야생 소 같은 동물을 그렸습니다. 흥미롭게도 사람 그림은 거의 없습니다. 그럼 그 옛날 어두운 동굴에서 어떻게 그림을 그렸을까요? 자연 재료로 색을 만들었습니다. 빨강과 노랑은 땅속 광물에서, 검정은 숯에서 얻었습니다. 이 가루를 물이나 동물 기름과 섞었습니다. 어떤 물감은 동물 털로 만든 붓으로 칠했고, 어떤 물감은 속이 빈 뼈로 불어서 뿌렸는데, 스프레이와 조금 비슷했죠. 빛을 얻으려고 작은 돌 등잔에 동물 기름을 태웠습니다. 안타깝게도 동굴이 일반에 공개된 뒤 수천 명 관람객의 숨이 동굴 안 공기를 바꾸어 그림이 손상되기 시작했습니다. 그래서 동굴은 1963년에 폐쇄되었습니다. 오늘날 관람객은 근처에 지은 매우 정교한 복제 동굴을 볼 수 있습니다.

script: Let's talk about prices. Why does the price of something go up or down? Economists usually answer this question with two ideas: supply and demand. Supply is how much of a product is available. Demand is how much people want to buy it. Let me give you a simple example. Imagine a small town with one shop that sells umbrellas. On sunny days, few people want umbrellas, so demand is low. If the shop wants to sell any, it may need to lower the price. Now imagine a week of heavy rain. Suddenly, everyone wants an umbrella. Demand goes up, but the shop still has the same number of umbrellas. Because there are more buyers than umbrellas, the shop can raise the price, and people will still pay. Supply can change, too. Let's say a problem at the factory means the shop gets only half its usual number of umbrellas. With fewer umbrellas available, the price usually goes up, even if demand doesn't change. The price where the amount people want to buy equals the amount available is called the equilibrium price. We'll draw graphs of this on Wednesday, so please read chapter three before then.

translation: 가격에 대해 이야기해 봅시다. 물건 가격은 왜 오르거나 내릴까요? 경제학자들은 보통 이 질문에 두 가지 개념, 공급과 수요로 답합니다. 공급은 상품이 얼마나 있는지이고, 수요는 사람들이 그것을 얼마나 사고 싶어 하는지입니다. 간단한 예를 들어 보죠. 우산을 파는 가게가 하나 있는 작은 마을을 상상해 보세요. 맑은 날에는 우산을 원하는 사람이 적으니 수요가 낮습니다. 가게가 조금이라도 팔려면 가격을 내려야 할 수도 있습니다. 이제 일주일 내내 폭우가 온다고 상상해 보세요. 갑자기 모두가 우산을 원합니다. 수요는 올라가지만 가게의 우산 수는 그대로입니다. 우산보다 사려는 사람이 많으니 가게는 가격을 올릴 수 있고, 사람들은 그래도 삽니다. 공급도 바뀔 수 있습니다. 공장에 문제가 생겨서 가게에 평소의 절반만 들어온다고 합시다. 구할 수 있는 우산이 적어지면 수요가 변하지 않아도 보통 가격이 오릅니다. 사람들이 사려는 양과 구할 수 있는 양이 같아지는 가격을 균형 가격이라고 합니다. 수요일에 이것을 그래프로 그려 볼 테니 그 전에 3장을 읽어 오세요.

script: In anthropology, we study how people in different cultures build relationships. One of the most important tools for this is something very ordinary: giving gifts. Now, you might think a gift is simply free. Someone gives you something, and that's the end of it. But anthropologists have found that in almost every culture, a gift creates an obligation. When you receive a gift, you're expected to give something back later. A French scholar named Marcel Mauss wrote about this about a hundred years ago. He described three duties: the duty to give, the duty to receive, and the duty to return. Think about your own life. If a friend invites you to dinner several times, and you never invite them back, how would they feel? Probably uncomfortable, right? The friendship might even end. Interestingly, the return gift usually shouldn't come right away. If your friend gives you a birthday present and you immediately hand them money for it, it feels like a business deal, not a friendship. The time between the gift and the return is what keeps people connected. In other words, a little bit of debt can actually be good for a relationship.

translation: 인류학에서는 여러 문화의 사람들이 어떻게 관계를 쌓는지 연구합니다. 이를 위한 가장 중요한 도구 중 하나는 아주 평범한 것, 바로 선물 주기입니다. 여러분은 선물이 그냥 공짜라고 생각할지도 모릅니다. 누가 무언가를 주면 그걸로 끝이라고요. 하지만 인류학자들은 거의 모든 문화에서 선물이 의무를 만든다는 것을 발견했습니다. 선물을 받으면 나중에 무언가를 되돌려 줄 것을 기대받습니다. 마르셀 모스라는 프랑스 학자가 약 100년 전에 이에 대해 썼습니다. 그는 세 가지 의무를 말했습니다. 줄 의무, 받을 의무, 되갚을 의무입니다. 여러분의 생활을 생각해 보세요. 친구가 여러분을 여러 번 저녁에 초대했는데 여러분이 한 번도 초대하지 않으면 친구는 어떤 기분일까요? 아마 불편하겠죠? 우정이 끝날 수도 있습니다. 흥미롭게도 답례는 보통 바로 하면 안 됩니다. 친구가 생일 선물을 주었는데 바로 그 값을 돈으로 건넨다면 우정이 아니라 거래처럼 느껴집니다. 선물과 답례 사이의 시간이 사람들을 이어 주는 것입니다. 다시 말해 약간의 빚은 오히려 관계에 좋을 수 있습니다.

script: Today, we're looking at how skyscrapers became possible. Before the late eighteen hundreds, most buildings in cities were no taller than five or six stories. There were two big reasons. The first was walls. In older buildings, the walls carried the weight of the whole building. The taller the building, the thicker the walls at the bottom needed to be. At some point, the walls on the ground floor became so thick that there was almost no room left inside. The second reason was stairs. Would you want to climb twenty floors every day? Probably not. So two inventions changed everything. The first was the steel frame. Instead of the walls holding the building up, a skeleton of steel beams did the job. The walls just hung on the frame, so they could be thin and full of windows. The second invention was the safe passenger elevator. Elevators existed before, but people were afraid the rope would break. In 1854, Elisha Otis showed an elevator with a safety brake that stopped it from falling. Once people trusted elevators, the top floors became the most popular, and most expensive, places to be. Soon, Chicago and New York started building upward.

translation: 오늘은 고층 빌딩이 어떻게 가능해졌는지 살펴보겠습니다. 1800년대 후반 이전에는 도시의 건물 대부분이 5~6층을 넘지 않았습니다. 두 가지 큰 이유가 있었습니다. 첫째는 벽입니다. 옛날 건물에서는 벽이 건물 전체의 무게를 지탱했습니다. 건물이 높을수록 아래쪽 벽이 더 두꺼워야 했습니다. 어느 순간 1층 벽이 너무 두꺼워져서 안에 공간이 거의 남지 않게 됩니다. 둘째 이유는 계단이었습니다. 매일 20층을 올라가고 싶나요? 아마 아니겠죠. 그래서 두 가지 발명이 모든 것을 바꿨습니다. 첫째는 철골 구조입니다. 벽이 건물을 받치는 대신 강철 보로 된 뼈대가 그 일을 했습니다. 벽은 뼈대에 매달려 있기만 해서 얇게 만들고 창문을 많이 낼 수 있었습니다. 두 번째 발명은 안전한 승객용 엘리베이터였습니다. 엘리베이터는 전에도 있었지만 사람들은 줄이 끊어질까 봐 두려워했습니다. 1854년 엘리샤 오티스가 떨어지지 않게 막는 안전 브레이크가 달린 엘리베이터를 선보였습니다. 사람들이 엘리베이터를 믿게 되자 꼭대기 층이 가장 인기 있고 가장 비싼 곳이 되었습니다. 곧 시카고와 뉴욕이 위로 건물을 올리기 시작했습니다.

script: Hello, everyone. This is an announcement from the Registrar's Office regarding course registration for the spring term. script: So far we've looked at how languages change slowly over centuries. Today I want to look at a case where a new language can appear surprisingly quickly. Imagine groups of people who don't share a language but need to communicate regularly, usually for trade or work. This happened often on plantations and in port cities during the colonial period. What develops in these situations is called a pidgin. A pidgin is a simplified way of speaking. It usually takes most of its vocabulary from one dominant language, but the grammar is stripped down. There might be no verb endings, no articles, and a fairly small set of words. Importantly, a pidgin has no native speakers. Everyone who uses it learned another language first, and they use the pidgin only for limited purposes. Now here's where it gets interesting. When children grow up in a community where the pidgin is the main shared language, they don't just copy it. They expand it. Within a generation or two, it develops consistent grammar, like ways of marking tense, and a much richer vocabulary. At that point, linguists call it a creole. Haitian Creole, for example, is spoken by millions of people and is a full, complex language in every sense. This tells us something remarkable about children: they don't simply imitate the language around them. They seem to actively build a system out of it.

questions.q: What is the lecture mainly about?
choices: How colonial governments chose official languages
Why some languages disappear over time
How pidgins form and develop into creoles
Why children learn foreign languages faster than adults

It has a large and complex vocabulary.
No one speaks it as a first language.

translation: 지금까지 우리는 언어가 수백 년에 걸쳐 천천히 변하는 방식을 살펴봤습니다. 오늘은 새로운 언어가 놀랄 만큼 빨리 생길 수 있는 경우를 보고 싶습니다. 공통 언어가 없는데 보통 무역이나 일 때문에 정기적으로 소통해야 하는 사람들의 무리를 상상해 보세요. 식민지 시대의 대농장과 항구 도시에서 이런 일이 자주 있었습니다. 이런 상황에서 생겨나는 것을 피진이라고 합니다. 피진은 단순화된 말하기 방식입니다. 보통 어휘 대부분을 한 지배적인 언어에서 가져오지만 문법은 대폭 줄어듭니다. 동사 어미도, 관사도 없고 단어 수도 꽤 적을 수 있습니다. 중요한 점은 피진에는 모국어 화자가 없다는 것입니다. 사용하는 사람 모두가 다른 언어를 먼저 배웠고, 피진은 제한된 목적으로만 씁니다. 이제 흥미로운 부분입니다. 피진이 주된 공통 언어인 공동체에서 아이들이 자라면, 아이들은 그것을 그냥 따라 하지 않습니다. 확장합니다. 한두 세대 안에 시제를 나타내는 방법 같은 일관된 문법과 훨씬 풍부한 어휘가 생깁니다. 그 시점에서 언어학자들은 그것을 크리올이라고 부릅니다. 예를 들어 아이티 크리올은 수백만 명이 쓰며 모든 의미에서 완전하고 복잡한 언어입니다. 이것은 아이들에 대해 놀라운 사실을 알려 줍니다. 아이들은 주변 언어를 단순히 흉내 내는 것이 아니라, 거기서 능동적으로 체계를 만들어 내는 것으로 보입니다.

script: Let's continue our discussion of camouflage. Last time, we talked about animals that match the color of their background, like a green frog sitting on a green leaf. Today, I want to introduce a more subtle trick called countershading. If you look at many fish, like sharks or mackerel, you'll notice that their backs are dark, but their bellies are pale, almost white. Deer, penguins, and lots of birds show the same pattern. At first, this seems strange. Why have two different colors? Wouldn't one color be better for hiding? Well, think about how light works in nature. Light usually comes from above, from the sun. So the top of any object is brightly lit, and the bottom is in shadow. That shadow is actually one of the main ways our eyes recognize a three-dimensional shape. Countershading cancels out that effect. The dark back absorbs some of the bright light on top, and the pale belly brightens the shadowed area below. The result is that the animal looks flat, and its shape is harder to pick out. For a fish in the ocean, there's even a second advantage. A predator looking down sees a dark back against the dark deep water. A predator looking up sees a pale belly against the bright surface. An American artist named Abbott Thayer described this principle over a century ago, and today it's sometimes called Thayer's law.

Why fish change color as they grow
How a two-tone coloring pattern helps animals hide
Why artists became interested in animals

translation: 위장에 대한 논의를 이어 갑시다. 지난 시간에는 초록 잎 위에 앉은 초록 개구리처럼 배경색과 맞추는 동물들을 이야기했습니다. 오늘은 역그늘 위장(countershading)이라는 더 미묘한 방법을 소개하고 싶습니다. 상어나 고등어 같은 많은 물고기를 보면 등은 어둡고 배는 거의 흰색에 가까울 만큼 밝다는 걸 알 수 있습니다. 사슴, 펭귄, 많은 새들도 같은 무늬를 보입니다. 처음에는 이상해 보입니다. 왜 색이 두 가지일까요? 숨기에는 한 가지 색이 더 낫지 않을까요? 자연에서 빛이 어떻게 작용하는지 생각해 보세요. 빛은 보통 위에서, 태양에서 옵니다. 그래서 어떤 물체든 윗면은 밝게 비치고 아랫면은 그늘이 집니다. 그 그림자는 사실 우리 눈이 입체 형태를 알아보는 주된 방법 중 하나입니다. 역그늘 위장은 그 효과를 상쇄합니다. 어두운 등은 위에서 오는 밝은 빛을 일부 흡수하고, 밝은 배는 아래 그늘진 부분을 밝게 해 줍니다. 그 결과 동물이 평평하게 보이고 형태를 알아보기 어려워집니다. 바다의 물고기에게는 두 번째 이점도 있습니다. 위에서 내려다보는 포식자에게는 어두운 등이 어두운 깊은 물을 배경으로 보입니다. 아래에서 올려다보는 포식자에게는 밝은 배가 밝은 수면을 배경으로 보입니다. 애벗 세이어라는 미국 화가가 100여 년 전에 이 원리를 설명했고, 오늘날 이를 세이어의 법칙이라고 부르기도 합니다.

script: Imagine you're walking through a field in, let's say, New England, and you come across a huge boulder sitting all by itself. It's the size of a car, and it's made of granite. But the bedrock underneath it and all around it is limestone. So how did it get there? For a long time, this was a real puzzle. Some people in the eighteenth century believed these rocks had been carried by giant floods. Today, geologists call these stones glacial erratics, and the name gives away the answer. The word erratic comes from a Latin word meaning to wander. During the last ice age, huge sheets of ice covered much of North America and northern Europe. As the glaciers moved, they scraped up rocks and carried them along, sometimes for hundreds of kilometers. When the climate warmed and the ice melted, the rocks were simply left behind wherever they happened to be. What makes erratics so useful to scientists is that they can often be traced back to their source. If a geologist finds an unusual type of granite in a field, and that granite only occurs in one particular mountain range, then we know the ice must have moved from that mountain range to this spot. By mapping many erratics, researchers can reconstruct the direction and size of ancient ice sheets. So a single rock sitting in a field is actually a record of climate history.

How granite and limestone are formed
Why floods were common in the eighteenth century

To explain how glaciers melted

questions.explanation: 특정 산맥에서만 나는 화강암이 들판에 있다면 얼음이 그 산맥에서 이곳으로 이동했음을 알 수 있다고 했습니다. 여러 표석을 지도로 그리면 빙상의 방향과 규모를 재구성할 수 있습니다.

translation: 예를 들어 뉴잉글랜드의 한 들판을 걷다가 홀로 놓인 거대한 바위를 만났다고 상상해 보세요. 자동차만 한 크기이고 화강암으로 되어 있습니다. 그런데 그 아래와 주변의 기반암은 석회암입니다. 그럼 이 바위는 어떻게 거기에 왔을까요? 오랫동안 이것은 진짜 수수께끼였습니다. 18세기의 어떤 사람들은 이 바위들이 거대한 홍수에 실려 왔다고 믿었습니다. 오늘날 지질학자들은 이런 돌을 빙하 표석(glacial erratic)이라고 부르는데, 이름이 답을 알려 줍니다. erratic이라는 말은 '떠돌다'라는 뜻의 라틴어에서 왔습니다. 마지막 빙하기 동안 거대한 빙상이 북아메리카와 북유럽의 상당 부분을 덮었습니다. 빙하가 움직이면서 바위를 긁어 올려 함께 옮겼고, 때로는 수백 킬로미터를 옮기기도 했습니다. 기후가 따뜻해져 얼음이 녹자 바위들은 우연히 놓인 곳에 그냥 남겨졌습니다. 표석이 과학자들에게 그렇게 유용한 이유는 원래 있던 곳을 추적할 수 있는 경우가 많기 때문입니다. 지질학자가 들판에서 특이한 종류의 화강암을 발견했는데 그 화강암이 한 특정 산맥에서만 난다면, 얼음이 그 산맥에서 이곳까지 이동했다는 것을 알 수 있습니다. 많은 표석을 지도에 표시하면 고대 빙상의 이동 방향과 크기를 재구성할 수 있습니다. 그러니 들판에 놓인 바위 하나가 사실은 기후 역사의 기록인 셈입니다.

script: Up until the 1990s, astronomers had never confirmed a single planet outside our solar system. Today, we know of more than five thousand. So what changed? Mostly, we got better at detecting tiny changes in starlight. Let me explain the most productive technique, which is called the transit method. The problem with finding exoplanets is that they're incredibly faint compared to their stars. Trying to see one directly is like trying to spot a firefly next to a stadium light from miles away. So instead of looking for the planet itself, astronomers watch the star. If a planet's orbit happens to line up with our view, then once every orbit, the planet passes in front of the star. When it does, it blocks a tiny fraction of the starlight. The star gets slightly dimmer, then returns to normal. By measuring how much the light drops, we can estimate the size of the planet. A bigger planet blocks more light. And by timing how often the dimming repeats, we learn how long the planet takes to orbit, which tells us how far it is from its star. Now, the method does have a limitation. It only works if the orbit is lined up edge-on from our point of view. Most planetary systems are tilted at some other angle, so we miss them entirely. That means for every planet we detect this way, there are probably many more we can't see.

Why stars change their brightness over time
How to photograph planets directly

The distance between the planet and its star
The age of the star
The size of the planet

choices: Only large planets can have stable orbits.
Most of them have already been discovered.

Most of them orbit edge-on to Earth.
questions.explanation: 대부분의 행성계는 기울어져 있어 통과 방법으로는 놓친다고 했고, 발견한 행성 하나마다 보지 못한 행성이 더 많을 것이라고 말합니다. 즉 실제 외계 행성 수는 발견된 수보다 훨씬 많다는 뜻입니다.

translation: 1990년대까지 천문학자들은 태양계 밖의 행성을 단 하나도 확인하지 못했습니다. 오늘날 우리는 5천 개가 넘는 행성을 알고 있습니다. 그럼 무엇이 달라졌을까요? 주로 별빛의 아주 작은 변화를 감지하는 능력이 좋아졌습니다. 가장 성과가 큰 기법인 통과(transit) 방법을 설명하겠습니다. 외계 행성을 찾기 어려운 이유는 행성이 자기 별에 비해 엄청나게 희미하기 때문입니다. 행성을 직접 보려는 것은 몇 킬로미터 떨어진 곳에서 경기장 조명 옆의 반딧불이를 찾으려는 것과 같습니다. 그래서 천문학자들은 행성 자체를 찾는 대신 별을 관찰합니다. 행성의 궤도가 우연히 우리 시선과 나란하면, 행성은 한 바퀴 돌 때마다 한 번씩 별 앞을 지나갑니다. 그때 별빛의 아주 작은 일부를 가립니다. 별이 약간 어두워졌다가 다시 원래대로 돌아옵니다. 빛이 얼마나 줄어드는지 측정하면 행성의 크기를 추정할 수 있습니다. 큰 행성일수록 빛을 더 많이 가리니까요. 그리고 어두워짐이 얼마나 자주 반복되는지 재면 행성이 한 바퀴 도는 데 걸리는 시간을 알 수 있고, 그것으로 별에서 얼마나 떨어져 있는지 알 수 있습니다. 하지만 이 방법에는 한계가 있습니다. 우리 쪽에서 볼 때 궤도가 정확히 옆면으로 보일 때만 통합니다. 대부분의 행성계는 다른 각도로 기울어져 있어서 아예 놓치게 됩니다. 즉 이 방법으로 행성 하나를 발견할 때마다 우리가 볼 수 없는 행성이 아마 훨씬 더 많이 있다는 뜻입니다.

script: Today's topic is something that should matter to every student in this room: how to study so that you actually remember things. More than a century ago, a German psychologist named Hermann Ebbinghaus ran a series of memory experiments on himself. He memorized lists of nonsense syllables, short made-up sounds with no meaning, and then tested himself after different amounts of time. He found that we forget new information very quickly at first, and then more slowly. This pattern is known as the forgetting curve. But Ebbinghaus found something else that's even more useful. When he spread his practice sessions out over several days, he needed far less total study time to learn a list than when he crammed all the practice into one session. This is called the spacing effect, and it's one of the most reliable findings in all of psychology. Why does it work? One explanation is that when you return to material after a gap, you've forgotten a little, so your brain has to work harder to retrieve it. That effort strengthens the memory. Cramming, by contrast, feels productive because the information is fresh in your mind, but that feeling of fluency is misleading. It tells you what you know right now, not what you'll know next week. Ironically, the method that feels easier is often the one that produces weaker learning.

choices: How to prepare for an exam in one night
How Ebbinghaus became a famous psychologist
Why nonsense syllables are hard to remember
Why spreading out study sessions improves memory

A method for spreading study over several days

A pattern of fast forgetting at first, then slower forgetting
questions.explanation: 새 정보를 처음에는 매우 빨리 잊고 그다음에는 더 천천히 잊는 패턴을 망각 곡선이라고 했습니다. 공부를 나누는 것은 간격 효과입니다.

questions.q: What does the professor mean when he says the feeling of fluency is misleading?
choices: Fluent speakers often forget grammar rules.
Students who read quickly usually understand less.
Cramming is always impossible for most students.
Feeling that material is easy now does not mean it will be remembered later.
questions.explanation: 교수는 벼락치기가 지금 알고 있는 것을 보여 줄 뿐 다음 주에 알고 있을 것을 보여 주지 않는다고 설명합니다. 지금 쉽게 느껴지는 것이 장기 기억을 보장하지 않는다는 뜻입니다.

questions.q: What can be inferred about the difficulty of recalling material after a break?
choices: It means the student should stop studying that material.
It shows that the student studied poorly.
It actually helps make the memory stronger.
It happens only with meaningless information.

translation: 오늘의 주제는 이 강의실의 모든 학생에게 중요할 내용, 실제로 기억에 남도록 공부하는 방법입니다. 100여 년 전, 헤르만 에빙하우스라는 독일 심리학자가 자기 자신을 대상으로 일련의 기억 실험을 했습니다. 그는 의미 없는 음절, 즉 뜻이 없는 짧은 만든 소리들의 목록을 외운 다음 여러 시간 간격을 두고 스스로 시험했습니다. 그 결과 우리는 새 정보를 처음에는 매우 빨리 잊고 그다음에는 더 천천히 잊는다는 것을 발견했습니다. 이 패턴을 망각 곡선이라고 합니다. 하지만 에빙하우스는 훨씬 더 유용한 것도 발견했습니다. 연습을 며칠에 걸쳐 나누어 했을 때, 한 번에 몰아서 했을 때보다 목록을 익히는 데 필요한 총 공부 시간이 훨씬 적었습니다. 이것을 간격 효과라고 하며, 심리학 전체에서 가장 믿을 만한 발견 중 하나입니다. 왜 효과가 있을까요? 한 가지 설명은, 간격을 두고 다시 공부하면 조금 잊어버린 상태라서 뇌가 그것을 떠올리려고 더 애써야 한다는 것입니다. 그 노력이 기억을 강화합니다. 반면 벼락치기는 정보가 머릿속에 생생해서 생산적으로 느껴지지만, 그 술술 되는 느낌은 착각입니다. 그 느낌은 지금 무엇을 아는지 알려 줄 뿐, 다음 주에 무엇을 알고 있을지는 알려 주지 않습니다. 아이러니하게도 더 쉽게 느껴지는 방법이 더 약한 학습을 낳는 경우가 많습니다.

script: Good morning. This message is from Information Technology Services. To strengthen security across campus systems, multi-factor authentication will become mandatory for all student accounts on March first. After that date, logging into email, the learning management system, or the library databases will require both your password and a code generated by the authenticator app on your phone. Roughly forty percent of students have already enrolled voluntarily. If you haven't, we'd urge you not to wait until the deadline, since the help desk anticipates a considerable backlog that week. Students without a smartphone can request a small hardware key from the IT office in Baker Hall at no cost. Please be aware that ITS staff will never ask for your password or authentication codes by email or phone. Any such request should be reported immediately.

To announce that campus email will be replaced
To inform students that an extra login step will soon be required
To recruit students to work at the help desk
questions.explanation: 3월 1일부터 모든 학생 계정에 다단계 인증이 의무화되어 비밀번호와 앱 코드가 함께 필요하다는 공지입니다. 도서관 데이터베이스는 적용 대상의 예일 뿐입니다.

questions.q: Why does the speaker say that ITS staff will never ask for passwords by email or phone?

To tell students to contact Baker Hall in person

translation: 안녕하세요. 정보기술지원팀(ITS)에서 알려 드립니다. 캠퍼스 전체 시스템의 보안을 강화하기 위해 3월 1일부터 모든 학생 계정에 다단계 인증이 의무화됩니다. 그날 이후 이메일, 학습관리시스템, 도서관 데이터베이스에 로그인하려면 비밀번호와 함께 휴대폰의 인증 앱이 만든 코드가 필요합니다. 이미 학생의 약 40%가 자발적으로 등록했습니다. 아직 등록하지 않았다면 마감일까지 기다리지 않기를 강력히 권합니다. 그 주에는 헬프데스크에 상당한 업무 적체가 예상되기 때문입니다. 스마트폰이 없는 학생은 베이커 홀 IT 사무실에서 소형 하드웨어 키를 무료로 신청할 수 있습니다. ITS 직원은 절대 이메일이나 전화로 비밀번호나 인증 코드를 요구하지 않는다는 점을 알아 두세요. 그런 요청을 받으면 즉시 신고해야 합니다.

script: Attention, undergraduate researchers. The Office of Undergraduate Research is now accepting proposals for the spring Research Symposium, which will be held on April twelfth in the Hamilton Conference Center. Students from every discipline, including the arts and humanities, are encouraged to apply. Proposals should include a title, a two-hundred-fifty-word abstract, and the name of a faculty mentor who has agreed to supervise your preparation. Presentations can be either a ten-minute talk or a poster. Note that projects still in progress are perfectly acceptable, provided you can present preliminary findings or a clearly defined method. The deadline is February twentieth at five p.m., and late submissions won't be considered under any circumstances. Last year, several presenters were approached by graduate programs afterward, so this is an excellent opportunity to gain visibility beyond your own department.

A complete set of final results
The name of a faculty member who has agreed to be a mentor

translation: 학부 연구생 여러분, 주목해 주세요. 학부연구지원실에서 4월 12일 해밀턴 컨퍼런스 센터에서 열리는 봄 연구 발표회의 발표 제안서를 받고 있습니다. 예술과 인문학을 포함한 모든 전공의 학생이 지원하기를 권합니다. 제안서에는 제목, 250단어 분량의 초록, 그리고 발표 준비를 지도하기로 동의한 지도 교수의 이름이 들어가야 합니다. 발표는 10분 구두 발표나 포스터 중 하나로 할 수 있습니다. 예비 결과나 명확하게 정의된 연구 방법을 제시할 수 있다면 아직 진행 중인 연구도 전혀 문제없습니다. 마감은 2월 20일 오후 5시이며, 늦게 낸 제안서는 어떤 경우에도 검토하지 않습니다. 작년에는 여러 발표자가 발표 후 대학원 과정으로부터 연락을 받았으니, 소속 학과를 넘어 자신을 알릴 수 있는 훌륭한 기회입니다.

script: Hello, everyone. The Fisher Library will undergo a major renovation beginning in June, and the building will be closed for approximately eighteen months. Here's how services will continue. The most frequently used books and all course reserves will be moved to a temporary library on the second floor of the Student Union. The remainder of the collection will be placed in off-site storage, but that doesn't mean it's inaccessible. You can request any stored item through the online catalog, and it'll typically arrive within forty-eight hours. Group study space will be more limited, so the university has extended the hours of several classroom buildings for evening study. We're also holding an open forum next Tuesday, where students can review the architects' plans and suggest features they'd like to see in the renovated building.

questions.explanation: 피셔 도서관이 18개월간 문을 닫는 동안 임시 도서관, 외부 보관 자료 신청, 스터디 공간 등 서비스가 어떻게 이어지는지 설명하는 공지입니다.

To reassure students that they can still get stored books

script: In 1968, the ecologist Garrett Hardin published an essay called The Tragedy of the Commons, and it became one of the most cited ideas in the social sciences. Hardin asked us to imagine a pasture open to all herders. Each herder gains the full benefit of adding one more cow, while the cost, the damage to the shared grass, is spread among everyone. So each person, acting rationally, keeps adding animals until the pasture is destroyed. Hardin's conclusion was fairly bleak: shared resources would inevitably be overused unless they were either privatized or controlled by a central government. It's a compelling argument, and it does describe some real situations, like overfishing in international waters. But the political economist Elinor Ostrom noticed that it didn't match what she observed in the field. She studied communities that had managed shared resources, such as irrigation systems in Spain and forests in Japan, for, in some cases, centuries, without either privatization or top-down control. What these communities had in common were institutions they'd designed themselves: clear boundaries on who could use the resource, rules adapted to local conditions, ways of monitoring one another, and graduated penalties, so that a first violation might bring a small fine rather than expulsion. In other words, the tragedy wasn't inevitable. It depended on whether users could communicate and build trust. Ostrom received the Nobel Prize in economics in 2009, the first woman to do so, largely for this work.

script: When we talk about why Impressionism emerged in France in the 1860s and 70s, we usually focus on artistic motives: painters like Monet and Renoir rebelling against the rigid conventions of the official Salon, wanting to capture fleeting effects of light rather than polished historical scenes. And that's all true. But I'd like to draw your attention to a much more ordinary factor, a piece of technology. Before the 1840s, painters generally bought pigments as powder, or even ground them themselves, and mixed them with oil in the studio. Prepared paint was stored in pig bladders, which were tied shut and punctured with a tack when you needed some. As you can imagine, they leaked, burst, and dried out quickly. That made painting outdoors for any length of time impractical, so landscapes were typically sketched outside and then finished in the studio. In 1841, an American portrait painter named John Goffe Rand patented the collapsible metal paint tube, essentially the kind of tube you still buy today. It was sealable, portable, and kept paint fresh. Combined with brighter synthetic pigments and the portable easel, this made it possible to complete an entire painting outdoors, directly in front of the subject. Renoir reportedly said that without paint in tubes, there would have been no Impressionism. Now, we shouldn't overstate this. Technology didn't cause Impressionism. Plenty of painters had tubes and kept working in studios. But it removed a practical barrier, and it made a certain kind of painting, quick and spontaneous, suddenly feasible.

script: On a summer afternoon, the center of a large city can be several degrees hotter than the surrounding countryside, and at night the difference can be even greater, sometimes as much as ten degrees Celsius. This phenomenon is known as the urban heat island effect. There are several contributing causes. The first involves materials. Asphalt and concrete absorb a great deal of solar energy during the day and release it slowly after sunset, which is why the nighttime gap tends to be so large. The second is the lack of vegetation. Plants cool their surroundings through a process called evapotranspiration, which essentially means that they release water vapor, and evaporation consumes heat. Replace a forest with parking lots, and you lose that natural air conditioning. Third, the geometry of the city matters. Tall buildings lining narrow streets create what are called urban canyons, which trap heat and block the wind. And finally, there's waste heat from cars, factories, and, ironically, air conditioners, which pump heat outdoors. Now, why does this matter beyond comfort? Heat waves are among the deadliest weather events, and their impact is concentrated in cities, particularly in low-income neighborhoods, which often have fewer trees and less access to cooling. Cities are responding in various ways. Some are painting roofs white or light gray to reflect sunlight. Others are investing heavily in green roofs and urban forests. These strategies are relatively inexpensive compared with the health costs of doing nothing.

script: If you've ever tuned a guitar or a piano, you've dealt with a problem that bothered musicians and mathematicians for more than two thousand years. The ancient Greeks, following Pythagoras, noticed that the most pleasing musical intervals correspond to simple ratios. If one string vibrates exactly twice as fast as another, you get an octave. A ratio of three to two gives you a perfect fifth, which sounds wonderfully stable. So you might think you could build an entire scale by stacking perfect fifths on top of each other. And that almost works. If you stack twelve perfect fifths, you should end up back at the same note, just seven octaves higher. But the math doesn't quite close. Twelve pure fifths overshoot seven octaves by a small amount, about a quarter of a semitone. This discrepancy is known as the Pythagorean comma. The practical consequence is that you can't tune a keyboard so that every interval is pure in every key. Over the centuries, musicians tried various compromises. The solution that eventually won out in the West is called equal temperament. Here, the octave is divided into twelve exactly equal semitones, so each fifth is made very slightly narrower than pure. The error is spread so evenly that most listeners barely notice. The great advantage is that you can move freely into any key, and everything sounds equally in tune. The cost, some would argue, is that every key now sounds equally slightly out of tune, and the distinctive character that different keys once had has largely disappeared.

translation: 기타나 피아노를 조율해 본 적이 있다면, 여러분은 2천 년 넘게 음악가와 수학자를 괴롭혀 온 문제를 다뤄 본 셈입니다. 고대 그리스인들은 피타고라스를 따라, 가장 듣기 좋은 음정이 단순한 비율에 대응한다는 것을 알아챘습니다. 한 줄이 다른 줄보다 정확히 두 배 빠르게 진동하면 옥타브가 됩니다. 3 대 2 비율은 완전 5도를 만드는데, 아주 안정적으로 들립니다. 그래서 완전 5도를 차곡차곡 쌓으면 음계 전체를 만들 수 있을 거라고 생각할 수 있습니다. 실제로 거의 됩니다. 완전 5도를 열두 번 쌓으면 같은 음으로, 다만 7옥타브 위로 돌아와야 합니다. 그런데 계산이 딱 맞아떨어지지 않습니다. 순정 5도 열두 개는 7옥타브를 조금, 반음의 약 4분의 1만큼 넘어섭니다. 이 차이를 피타고라스 콤마라고 합니다. 실제로 이것은 모든 조에서 모든 음정이 순정하도록 건반을 조율할 수 없다는 뜻입니다. 수 세기 동안 음악가들은 여러 타협안을 시도했습니다. 결국 서양에서 이긴 해법은 평균율이라고 불립니다. 평균율에서는 옥타브를 정확히 같은 반음 열두 개로 나누어, 각 5도를 순정보다 아주 약간 좁게 만듭니다. 오차가 아주 고르게 퍼져 있어서 대부분의 청자는 거의 알아채지 못합니다. 큰 장점은 어떤 조로든 자유롭게 옮겨 갈 수 있고 모든 것이 똑같이 맞게 들린다는 점입니다. 일부에서 주장하듯 그 대가는, 이제 모든 조가 똑같이 약간씩 음이 어긋나 들리고, 여러 조가 한때 지녔던 독특한 성격이 대부분 사라졌다는 것입니다.

script: Last week we looked at Romanesque churches, with their massive walls and small, deep-set windows. Today, I want to explain how Gothic builders in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries managed to create cathedrals that seem, by comparison, almost weightless, with soaring ceilings and enormous stained-glass windows. The key challenge is what engineers call lateral thrust. A stone vault, the arched ceiling, doesn't just push straight down on the walls. It also pushes outward, trying to spread the walls apart. The higher and wider the vault, the greater that outward push. Romanesque builders countered it with sheer mass: thick walls and few openings. Gothic builders took a different approach, combining three innovations. First, the pointed arch, which directs more of the force downward than a rounded arch does, reducing the outward push. Second, the ribbed vault, which channels the weight of the ceiling along stone ribs to specific points, rather than distributing it along the entire wall. And third, and most visibly, the flying buttress, an external arm of stone that reaches from the upper wall across to a heavy pier standing outside the building. It catches the thrust at exactly the point where it's concentrated and carries it safely to the ground. Once the forces were handled by this external skeleton, the wall between the supports no longer had to bear much load. It could be opened up and filled with glass. So the famous windows of Chartres are not just artistic achievements. In a sense, they're a consequence of structural engineering.

questions.q: What is the lecture mainly about?
choices: Why Romanesque churches had small windows
How Gothic builders solved a structural problem to build tall, bright churches
How stained glass was produced in the Middle Ages
The religious meaning of Gothic architecture

questions.q: What is lateral thrust?
choices: The outward push of a vault on the walls
The weight of the stained-glass windows
The downward force of a pointed arch
The pressure of wind against a tall building

They were added after the cathedral was completed.

translation: 지난주에는 거대한 벽과 작고 깊숙한 창을 가진 로마네스크 교회를 살펴봤습니다. 오늘은 12~13세기 고딕 건축가들이 어떻게 그에 비해 거의 무게가 없어 보이는, 높이 솟은 천장과 거대한 스테인드글라스 창을 가진 대성당을 만들 수 있었는지 설명하려 합니다. 핵심 과제는 공학자들이 횡추력이라고 부르는 것입니다. 아치형 천장인 돌 볼트는 벽을 수직으로만 누르지 않습니다. 바깥쪽으로도 밀어서 벽을 벌리려 합니다. 볼트가 높고 넓을수록 그 바깥으로 미는 힘이 커집니다. 로마네스크 건축가들은 순전히 질량, 즉 두꺼운 벽과 적은 개구부로 이에 맞섰습니다. 고딕 건축가들은 세 가지 혁신을 결합하는 다른 방법을 택했습니다. 첫째, 첨두아치입니다. 둥근 아치보다 힘을 더 많이 아래로 보내 바깥으로 미는 힘을 줄입니다. 둘째, 리브 볼트입니다. 천장 무게를 벽 전체에 퍼뜨리는 대신 돌 갈빗대를 따라 특정 지점으로 모읍니다. 셋째, 가장 눈에 띄는 플라잉 버트레스입니다. 위쪽 벽에서 건물 밖에 선 무거운 기둥까지 뻗은 돌로 된 바깥 팔입니다. 이것은 추력이 집중되는 바로 그 지점에서 힘을 받아 안전하게 땅으로 전달합니다. 이 외부 뼈대가 힘을 처리하게 되자, 지지대 사이의 벽은 더 이상 큰 하중을 질 필요가 없었습니다. 벽을 틔워서 유리로 채울 수 있었죠. 그러니 샤르트르 대성당의 유명한 창들은 단지 예술적 성취가 아닙니다. 어떤 의미에서는 구조 공학의 결과물입니다.

script: On behalf of the Provost's Office, I'd like to clarify the university's revised academic integrity policy concerning generative AI tools, which takes effect at the start of the spring term. Contrary to some reports on social media, the policy does not impose a blanket prohibition. Rather, it delegates authority to individual instructors, who must specify in their syllabi whether, and to what extent, such tools may be used in each assignment. Where a syllabus is silent, the default presumption is that use is not permitted. Students who are uncertain are expected to seek clarification in writing before submitting work, not after a concern has been raised. Undisclosed use in a course that requires disclosure will be treated as a violation, irrespective of how substantial the assistance was. Workshops explaining the policy will be offered through the library throughout January.

To announce that AI tools are banned in all courses
To correct a misunderstanding and explain how a new policy works
To promote a set of library workshops on writing

script: Attention, everyone. On Thursday at eleven a.m., Public Safety will conduct its semiannual test of the emergency notification system. script: A reminder about the Whitfield Fellowship, which supports one year of independent study abroad for graduating seniors. The selection committee has asked me to address a recurring misconception. The fellowship is not intended to fund enrollment in a degree program; applicants proposing a master's degree, however compelling, are routinely declined. What the committee is looking for is a self-directed project that couldn't be pursued as effectively at home, whether that's apprenticing with a craftsman, documenting an endangered dialect, or studying water management in the Netherlands. Grade point average is considered but isn't decisive. The committee places far more weight on the coherence of the proposal and on evidence that the applicant has laid meaningful groundwork, such as establishing contacts abroad. Campus nomination is required, so internal applications are due six weeks before the national deadline, on October first.

To explain how to apply to master's programs abroad

script: The idea that the language we speak shapes the way we think is usually associated with Benjamin Lee Whorf, and in its strongest form, sometimes called linguistic determinism, it holds that language actually constrains which thoughts are possible. If your language lacks a word for something, the argument goes, you can't conceive of it. That strong version has been thoroughly discredited. Speakers routinely grasp concepts their languages don't have single words for, and translation, however imperfect, would be impossible if languages sealed their speakers into separate worlds. But the rejection of determinism was, arguably, an overcorrection, because for decades the entire question was treated as unrespectable. What revived it was a shift in method: instead of speculating about worldviews, researchers began designing narrowly targeted experiments. Consider spatial reference. Speakers of Guugu Yimithirr, an Australian language, don't describe locations as left or right. They use compass directions, so they'd say there's an ant on your north leg. Studies found that these speakers maintain a remarkably accurate sense of orientation, even in unfamiliar buildings, which makes sense, since they can't speak correctly without knowing where north is. Or take color. Russian obligatorily distinguishes light blue from dark blue with two separate basic words. Russian speakers turn out to be measurably faster at telling apart shades that fall across that boundary, and, tellingly, the advantage disappears when they perform a simultaneous verbal task that occupies the language system. So the current consensus, if there is one, is a weak version: language doesn't imprison thought, but habitual patterns of speech appear to train attention, making certain distinctions more automatic.

questions.q: What is the lecture mainly about?
choices: How Australian and Russian languages developed
Why Whorf's theory was proven correct by modern experiments
How research has revived a limited form of the idea that language influences thought
Why translation between languages is always imperfect
questions.explanation: 교수는 강한 언어 결정론은 폐기되었지만 정교한 실험을 통해 '언어가 주의를 훈련한다'는 약한 형태의 언어 상대성이 되살아났다고 설명합니다. 휘프의 이론이 그대로 옳다고 증명된 것은 아닙니다.

questions.q: Why does the professor describe the rejection of linguistic determinism as an overcorrection?
choices: It caused researchers to dismiss even milder, testable versions of the idea for years.
It led researchers to accept the strong version too quickly.

script: We usually picture evolution as a branching tree. Genes pass vertically, from parent to offspring, and lineages split and diverge but never rejoin. For animals and plants, that picture is a reasonable approximation. For bacteria, however, it's misleading in a fairly fundamental way, because bacteria routinely acquire genes from organisms that aren't their ancestors, a process called horizontal gene transfer. There are three main routes. In transformation, a bacterium absorbs fragments of DNA released into the environment when other cells die. In transduction, viruses that infect bacteria accidentally package bits of host DNA and deliver them to the next cell they infect. And in conjugation, which is perhaps the most striking, one bacterium extends a thin tube to another and passes along a copy of a small loop of DNA called a plasmid. The clinical consequences are serious. Genes that provide antibiotic resistance are frequently carried on plasmids, which means resistance doesn't have to evolve independently in each species through the slow accumulation of mutations. It can spread sideways, across species boundaries, in a matter of hours. A harmless gut bacterium can serve as a reservoir, handing resistance to a dangerous pathogen. The theoretical consequences are just as profound. When researchers began sequencing whole bacterial genomes, they found that a substantial fraction of the genes in many species had been acquired horizontally. Some biologists now argue that near the base of life's history, the tree metaphor breaks down entirely, and what we have is something closer to a web, with lineages continually exchanging genetic material.

script: If you apply Newtonian gravity to a spiral galaxy, you arrive at a clear prediction. Most of the visible mass, the stars and gas, is concentrated toward the center. So stars far out in the disk should orbit more slowly than those closer in, just as Neptune orbits the Sun far more slowly than Mercury does. Plot orbital speed against distance from the center, what's called a rotation curve, and you'd expect it to rise near the core and then decline steadily. In the 1970s, Vera Rubin and Kent Ford measured these curves with unprecedented precision, and what they found was that they don't decline. They stay flat, far beyond the edge of the visible disk. Stars at the outskirts are moving so fast that, given the visible mass alone, they ought to fly off into intergalactic space. Now, logically, there are two ways to resolve this. Either there's a great deal of mass we can't see, or our law of gravity is wrong at these scales. The mainstream view adopted the first option: galaxies are embedded in vast halos of dark matter, which interacts gravitationally but doesn't emit or absorb light. It's worth emphasizing that dark matter is, at this point, inferred entirely from its gravitational effects. Decades of experiments designed to detect it directly have come up empty. That's why a minority of physicists continue to pursue modified gravity theories. The difficulty for them is that dark matter accounts for a remarkably diverse range of observations, from galaxy clusters to the early universe, whereas modified gravity tends to succeed in some areas and struggle in others.

script: In 1865, the English economist William Stanley Jevons published a book called The Coal Question. Britain's industrial power depended on coal, and people were worried about running out. A natural assumption was that more efficient steam engines, which get more work out of each ton of coal, would ease the problem by reducing consumption. Jevons argued exactly the opposite. Greater efficiency, he said, lowers the effective cost of using coal, which makes coal-powered processes profitable in applications where they previously weren't, and so total consumption rises. This counterintuitive claim is now known as the Jevons paradox. Contemporary economists usually discuss it under the broader heading of the rebound effect, and they're careful to distinguish degrees. If a more fuel-efficient car leads you to drive somewhat more, but your total fuel use still falls, that's a partial rebound. Some of the expected savings are eaten up, but not all. The full paradox, where consumption actually increases, which economists call backfire, requires particular conditions. Typically, the resource must represent a large share of the cost of the activity, and demand for that activity must be highly responsive to price. That's why the paradox seems to have held for coal in nineteenth-century Britain, and arguably for lighting over the past two centuries. But for, say, household refrigerators, the evidence points to modest rebounds. The policy lesson isn't that efficiency is futile. It's that efficiency on its own may be insufficient, and that it often needs to be paired with measures, like carbon pricing, that keep the effective cost of consumption from falling.

translation: 1865년 영국 경제학자 윌리엄 스탠리 제번스는 『석탄 문제』라는 책을 냈습니다. 영국의 산업력은 석탄에 달려 있었고, 사람들은 석탄이 바닥날까 걱정했습니다. 자연스러운 가정은, 석탄 1톤에서 더 많은 일을 뽑아내는 더 효율적인 증기기관이 소비를 줄여 문제를 덜어 줄 것이라는 것이었습니다. 제번스는 정확히 반대로 주장했습니다. 효율이 높아지면 석탄 사용의 실질 비용이 낮아져 전에는 수익이 나지 않던 분야에서도 석탄 동력 공정이 수익을 내게 되고, 그래서 총소비량이 늘어난다는 것이었죠. 이 직관에 반하는 주장은 오늘날 제번스 역설로 알려져 있습니다. 현대 경제학자들은 보통 이것을 더 넓은 개념인 반동 효과로 다루며, 정도를 신중하게 구분합니다. 연비가 더 좋은 차 때문에 운전을 좀 더 하게 되더라도 총연료 사용량이 여전히 줄어든다면, 그것은 부분 반동입니다. 예상한 절감의 일부는 사라지지만 전부는 아닙니다. 소비가 실제로 늘어나는 완전한 역설, 경제학자들이 역효과(backfire)라고 부르는 것은 특정한 조건이 필요합니다. 대개 그 자원이 해당 활동 비용에서 큰 몫을 차지해야 하고, 그 활동에 대한 수요가 가격에 매우 민감해야 합니다. 그래서 이 역설은 19세기 영국의 석탄에, 그리고 아마 지난 두 세기 동안의 조명에 들어맞았던 것으로 보입니다. 하지만 예컨대 가정용 냉장고의 경우 증거는 크지 않은 반동을 가리킵니다. 정책적 교훈은 효율이 헛되다는 것이 아닙니다. 효율만으로는 불충분할 수 있으며, 탄소 가격제처럼 소비의 실질 비용이 떨어지지 않게 하는 조치와 짝을 이뤄야 하는 경우가 많다는 것입니다.

script: Between roughly seven hundred and six hundred and thirty-five million years ago, Earth may have gone through the most extreme climate episodes in its history. According to the Snowball Earth hypothesis, ice sheets extended all the way to the equator, possibly covering the oceans almost entirely. The initial evidence was puzzling rather than conclusive. Geologists found glacial deposits, the characteristic jumble of rock scraped up and dumped by ice, in rock layers that, based on their magnetic signatures, must have formed near the equator. Now, you might ask why a global freeze wouldn't simply be permanent. That's actually the heart of the problem. Ice reflects most incoming sunlight, so once ice advances past a certain latitude, a runaway feedback sets in: more ice, more reflection, more cooling. Early climate models suggested that once the planet froze over, it could never thaw. The proposed escape is elegant. Volcanoes keep erupting regardless of the ice, releasing carbon dioxide. Ordinarily, that gas is gradually removed from the atmosphere through the chemical weathering of rocks, a process that depends on rain and exposed land. On a frozen planet, weathering essentially stops. So carbon dioxide builds up over millions of years, until the greenhouse effect is strong enough to overcome the reflectivity of the ice, and then the melting would be abrupt. Strikingly, glacial deposits from this era are often capped directly by thick layers of carbonate rock, which typically forms in warm water. That's exactly what you'd predict if a greenhouse atmosphere suddenly dumped its excess carbon into the oceans. Critics, however, favor a slushball version, with open water near the equator, which may have been necessary for early life to survive.

questions.q: What is the lecture mainly about?
choices: How volcanoes formed near the equator
A hypothesis about an ancient global freeze and how it may have ended
Why modern ice sheets are melting quickly
How early life first appeared in warm oceans
questions.explanation: 교수는 눈덩이 지구 가설의 증거, 얼음이 영구적이지 않았던 이유(화산 이산화탄소 축적), 그리고 비판적 견해를 설명합니다.

questions.q: Why were glacial deposits in certain rock layers significant?
choices: They showed that volcanoes had stopped erupting.
They contained fossils of early life.
The layers had formed near the equator, suggesting ice reached low latitudes.
They proved that the oceans never froze completely.
questions.explanation: 자기 특성으로 보아 적도 근처에서 형성된 암석층에서 빙하 퇴적물이 발견되었다고 했습니다. 이는 얼음이 적도 가까이까지 확장되었음을 시사하는 증거였습니다.

questions.q: Why does the professor mention the layers of carbonate rock?
choices: To show that the ice never reached the equator
To present evidence consistent with a sudden shift to a greenhouse climate
To explain how weathering removes carbon dioxide
To argue that the slushball version is correct
questions.explanation: 보통 따뜻한 물에서 생기는 탄산염암이 빙하 퇴적물 바로 위를 덮고 있다는 것은, 온실 대기가 과잉 탄소를 갑자기 바다로 쏟아 냈다는 예측과 정확히 맞는다고 했습니다. 급격한 해빙 시나리오를 뒷받침하는 증거로 든 것입니다.

questions.q: What can be inferred about the critics who favor the slushball version?
choices: They believe volcanoes stopped releasing carbon dioxide.
They reject the idea that ice ever reached low latitudes.
They think complete ice cover would have made it hard for life to survive.
They argue that the melting happened very slowly.
questions.explanation: 비판자들은 적도 부근에 열린 바다가 있는 '슬러시볼' 형태를 선호하며, 그 열린 물이 초기 생명의 생존에 필요했을 수 있다고 봅니다. 즉 완전한 결빙이었다면 생명이 살아남기 어려웠을 것이라는 문제의식을 가지고 있습니다.

translation: 대략 7억 년 전에서 6억 3,500만 년 전 사이에 지구는 역사상 가장 극단적인 기후 시기를 겪었을지 모릅니다. 눈덩이 지구 가설에 따르면 빙상이 적도까지 뻗어 나가 바다를 거의 완전히 덮었을 수도 있습니다. 처음의 증거는 결정적이라기보다 수수께끼 같았습니다. 지질학자들은 얼음이 긁어 와 쏟아 놓은 특유의 뒤섞인 암석, 즉 빙하 퇴적물을 발견했는데, 그것이 들어 있는 암석층이 자기적 특성으로 보아 적도 근처에서 형성된 것이 분명했습니다. 그렇다면 여러분은 지구 전체가 얼었는데 왜 영원히 얼어 있지 않았는지 물을 수 있습니다. 사실 그것이 문제의 핵심입니다. 얼음은 들어오는 햇빛 대부분을 반사하기 때문에, 얼음이 어떤 위도를 넘어 확장되면 폭주하는 되먹임이 시작됩니다. 얼음이 늘고, 반사가 늘고, 냉각이 심해지는 거죠. 초기 기후 모형들은 행성이 한번 얼어붙으면 절대 녹을 수 없다고 보았습니다. 제시된 탈출 방법은 우아합니다. 화산은 얼음과 상관없이 계속 분출하며 이산화탄소를 내뿜습니다. 평소에는 그 기체가 암석의 화학적 풍화로 대기에서 서서히 제거되는데, 이 과정은 비와 드러난 땅에 의존합니다. 얼어붙은 행성에서는 풍화가 사실상 멈춥니다. 그래서 이산화탄소가 수백만 년에 걸쳐 쌓이다가 온실 효과가 얼음의 반사율을 이길 만큼 강해지면, 해빙은 급격하게 일어났을 것입니다. 놀랍게도 이 시기의 빙하 퇴적물 바로 위를 두꺼운 탄산염암층이 덮고 있는 경우가 많은데, 탄산염암은 보통 따뜻한 물에서 만들어집니다. 온실 대기가 과잉 탄소를 갑자기 바다로 쏟아 냈다면 정확히 예상되는 결과입니다. 그러나 비판자들은 적도 근처에 열린 바다가 있었던 '슬러시볼' 형태를 선호하는데, 그런 열린 물이 초기 생명이 살아남는 데 필요했을 수 있기 때문입니다.
